discussions.name: NWS Seattle
synopsis: Precipitation chances will linger today as a weak system brings light rain to the lowlands and light snow to the Cascades. A weak ridge building over the Pacific Northwest will bring a brief break in precipitation this weekend. An active weather pattern resumes early next week with a series of systems moving across the region.
hydrology: River levels should continue to gradually fall with the Skokomish expected to recede below flood stage tonight. Additional rises to the Skokomish are possible next week with additional incoming precipitation, but a large degree of uncertainty remains over the extended forecast.

sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: Precipitation chances will linger today as a weak system brings light rain to the lowlands and light snow to the Cascades. A weak ridge building over the Pacific Northwest will bring a brief break in precipitation this weekend. An active weather pattern resumes early next week with a series of systems moving across the region.

sections.title: Short term (today through Sunday)
paragraphs: Precipitation associated with a stalled frontal boundary over Oregon will spread northward into the area later today, but it will be considerably lighter than what we saw on Thanksgiving morning. With a cooler air mass in place, we'll see some light snowfall in the passes. But it is expected to fall short of any headlines. Shortwave ridging will slide across the region late tonight into Saturday for a short reprieve from the recent active weather.

Another developing system moves into the offshore waters on Sunday with some rain spreading inland across Western Washington through the course of the day. Models do not have a good handle on the track and strength of the surface low. Parts of Western Washington will likely see windy conditions developing by Sunday night, but the path of the low will define a lot of the details. And we'll discuss that in the long term discussion.

Coastal flooding remains a threat for many areas heading into the weekend. Areas along the north interior coastline are favored to see the highest degree of coastal flooding over the weekend, with lesser impacts expected elsewhere.

sections.title: Long term (Sunday night through Thursday)
paragraphs: As alluded to in the short term discussion, the path of a surface low Sunday night into Monday could have significant implications in terms of the wind forecast. Models solutions range from a weakening surface low tracking into northern Vancouver Island to a concerning 00Z operational ECMWF showing a sub 985 millibar low making landfall over Grays Harbor county early Monday AM and tracking northeastward across the CWA. Stay tuned to the forecast as models get a better handle as to how this is expected to play out.

There is a trend toward a somewhat quieter period of weather as we move toward the middle of the coming week with the storm track diving southward into California. This pattern favors anomalous weak ridging just offshore. While this doesn't imply an entirely dry forecast, it does favor somewhat more benign conditions as systems moving into British Columbia clip the area.
Additional coastal flooding may occur into next week due to high astronomical tides.

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: Westerly flow aloft this morning as a weak system will move through western Washington late this morning and afternoon. Showers near OLM this morning, with rain lifting north and becoming widespread after 19Z. Rain activity will subside this evening. Majority of terminals remain VFR this morning. However, a few terminals are reporting MVFR to IFR. Ceilings will continue to lower with widespread MVFR by this afternoon, continuing into Saturday. S/SW winds 5-7 kt today, will become light to calm tonight into Saturday morning.

With light/calm winds tonight and residual moisture, there is a 60- 70% chance for visibility less than 1SM over the southern interior. However, there is uncertainty with Puget Sound terminals as fog development would be dependent on the amount of clearing behind today's system. Latest guidance suggests there is a 35-45% chance for visibility less than 1SM, especially in the valleys.

KSEA...MVFR this morning and will likely prevail into Saturday. Rain will start impacting the terminal around 19Z, which could reduce visibility to 4SM at times in heavier rain. Rain will subside this evening. S/SW winds 5-7 kt will become light this evening/tonight, introducing the potential for fog at terminal Saturday morning. While there is uncertainty on fog development due to sky cover, high-res guidance suggests there is a 35% chance for visibility below 1SM around 16Z. Winds will shift NE after 12Z Saturday at 3-5 kt.

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: Winds will continue throughout the day with Small Craft Advisories continuing for the coastal waters, mainly due to elevated seas. A weak system will approach the area waters today, with minimal impacts to wind and seas. High pressure will then develop over the coastal waters through the weekend, with wind and seas further easing. The exception is the Strait of Juan De Fuca, where a westerly push of winds is likely.

A low pressure looks to move into the area Monday into Tuesday, for increasing winds and seas. Latest guidance is a bit shaky on the exact tracking of the low pressure system, which could impact the strength of the winds. Will continue to monitor as more guidance becomes available.

Coastal seas generally 10 to 15 this morning decreasing to below 10 early this evening. Seas will decrease even further to 4 to 6 over the weekend, before the aforementioned system moves in on Monday, increasing seas upwards to 15 to 18 feet.
Mazurkiewicz

paragraphs: River levels should continue to gradually fall with the Skokomish expected to recede below flood stage tonight. Additional rises to the Skokomish are possible next week with additional incoming precipitation, but a large degree of uncertainty remains over the extended forecast.

discussions.name: NWS Portland
synopsis: Steady rain on Friday will end from north to south Friday night. Dry weather and offshore winds return Saturday. Active weather returns Sunday into Monday with rain and windy conditions. A break from rain and wind is expected late Tuesday into Wednesday before rain returns Wednesday night into Thursday.

sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: Steady rain on Friday will end from north to south Friday night. Dry weather and offshore winds return Saturday. Active weather returns Sunday into Monday with rain and windy conditions. A break from rain and wind is expected late Tuesday into Wednesday before rain returns Wednesday night into Thursday.

sections.title: Discussion
paragraphs: Now through Thursday night...Radar and surface weather observations from early Friday afternoon showed light to moderate rain continuing over northwest Oregon and southwest WA along a quasi-stationary front. Observed hourly rain rates have generally ranged between 0.01-0.10 in/hr, and have not been high enough to result in flooding. However, GOES-18 water vapor imagery showed an area of enhanced moisture over the coastal waters beginning to move inland. This will bring a period of relatively heavier rain with hourly rain rates as high as 0.1-0.25 in/hr between 2-6 PM. Rain rates could briefly exceed 0.25 in/hr within the Willamette Valley (25-45% chance over the central/southern valley). This may result in short-lived minor urban flooding in low-lying areas with poor drainage, along with some ponding on roads. Motorists should exercise caution for their evening commute as there will be an increased risk of hydroplaning. REFS guidance suggests rain will end from north to south after sunset Friday evening as the aforementioned frontal boundary begins to move southward. Given skies will be clearing out tonight with winds becoming calm and ground conditions remaining wet, chances will increase for fog development.

Dry weather returns for Saturday as upper level ridging moves inland, though don't expect much sunshine as high clouds will be increasing ahead of the next weather system. Specific details remain uncertain this far out, but what is clear is this system will bring additional widespread rain Sunday morning into Monday as well as increasing southerly winds Sunday night into Monday. The amount of moisture associated with this system is less than the previous two systems. Between 4 AM Sunday and 4 AM Tuesday, there remains a 40-60% chance for the interior lowlands to receive at least 1 inch of rain and a 30-50% chance for the coast and terrain to receive at least 2 inches of rain. Rain amounts of this magnitude falling within a 48-hour period suggests flooding is unlikely to occur. Wind is the primary concern late Sunday night into Monday morning as many ensemble members indicate the surface low strengthening as it approaches the north OR/south WA coast and moves north towards B.C. just along the coast line. The NBM indicates a 30-50% chance of peak wind gusts exceeding 58 mph (High Wind Warning criteria) along the immediate coast and for elevations above 1500 ft in the Coast Range and a 15-30% chance for inland coastal communities such as Astoria and Tillamook. There's also a 20-40% chance for peak wind gusts exceeding 45 mph (Wind Advisory criteria) in the Willamette Valley, Portland/Vancouver metro area, and Cascade foothills. Gusts of this strength would cause some degree of downed trees and power outages, especially as soils continue to saturate from continued weather systems. Although snow levels will likely fall below the Cascade passes Monday night into Tuesday, precipitation will be winding down at that time. Therefore, forecast snow amounts will most likely only reach a trace to one inch at pass level (70-80% chance for at least 0.1 inches of snow at Willamette and Santiam Passes, and a 30-40% along highway 26 near Government Camp). Chances for snow amounts over 1 inch have decreased to 5-10%. Therefore, significant travel impacts are not expected at pass level.

There's a 10-35% chance of light showers continuing into Tuesday morning and afternoon, mainly over higher terrain and along the coast, as a weak trough originating from Alaska with limited moisture moves through the PacNW. Colder air moves in behind this trough, dropping daytime temperatures into the mid 40s for the interior lowlands for Wednesday. Additionally, ensembles are confident in a period of dry weather Tuesday night through Wednesday afternoon with the arrival of a transient shortwave ridge. Dry weather is not expected to last long as ensembles indicate another weather system bringing more precipitation to the area sometime late Wednesday into Thursday. Ensemble guidance shows large model spread for QPF amounts during that time, however even the wettest ensemble guidance suggests flooding will not be a threat. The main impact with this system will be the potential for light snow accumulations at the Cascade passes (20-40% chance of at least 1" of snow between 4 PM Wednesday and 4 PM Thursday at pass level and a 10-20% chance for at least 3 inches). While this isn't very much snow given the time of year, it would be enough to result in minor travel impacts. -23/03

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: Through 00Z Sunday...Rain continues over the airspace as of 22Z Fri, bringing a mix of conditions to all terminals, varying from VFR to LIFR. Rain will become more widespread and intense through today, spreading from north to south. Expect this mixed bag of conditions to trend to mostly VFR/MVFR this evening (30-50%) and persist through tonight. Moderate to locally heavy rain at times may also lead to VIS reductions to 2-4 SM. As rain ends from north to south this evening/tonight, conditions may improve to VFR for inland terminals, generally after 03-07Z Sat. High cloud cover arrives tonight around 12Z Sat, introducing a bit of uncertainty regarding conditions overnight. Before these high clouds arrive, low status may develop and continue/develop MVFR/IFR CIGs, so forecasted CIGs entirely depend on the expected time of arrival of high clouds tonight. Conditions should improve back to VFR around 20Z Sat. Otherwise, expect northerly winds under 10 kts through the period.

KPDX AND APPROACHES...Rain continues until 04Z Sat, bringing a mix of VFR/MVFR conditions this afternoon. Heavier showers could produce brief IFR conditions. As rain ends around 04Z Sat, conditions are expected to improve to VFR although there is a 40-60% chance that MVFR conditions will persist overnight as overnight stratus may develop. Uncertainty remains beyond 06Z Sat as high clouds may move over the airspace around 12Z Sat, inhibiting low stratus development. Conditions should improve back to VFR around 20Z Sat. Expect northerly winds under 8 kts through the period. ~12

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: Current buoy observations as of Friday afternoon shows wave heights around 10-12 ft at 12-14 seconds with winds below 15 kts. Conditions will remain steady today as another weather system moves through the waters. A Small Craft Advisory remains in effect through 1 AM Saturday until seas fall below 10 ft.

A brief break in active weather will see calmer marine conditions on Saturday into early Sunday with seas falling to 5-7 ft. However, another weather system will impact the waters Sunday afternoon into early next week. There is 70-90% chance of gales Sunday night into Monday, with a brief 40-50% chance of storm force winds early Monday morning. A strong west to northwesterly swell then builds over the coastal waters associated with this weather system through Monday afternoon. Confidence is high (60-70% chance) wave heights exceed 15 ft again Monday morning and afternoon, with a 20-40% chance of exceeding 20 ft. ~12/03

sections.title: Beach hazards
paragraphs: The combination of King Tides and elevated seas leading to tidal overflow continue to support a Coastal Flood Advisory through high tide this afternoon for the south Washington coast, Clatsop County coast, and Tillamook County coast. Coastal residents in the warned area should be alert for rising water and take appropriate action to protect life and property. There is also a continued moderate to high sneaker wave threat through Friday as well. Beachgoers should exercise caution, stay far back from incoming waves, and remain observant of the ocean. Avoid logs, large rocks, and jetties.
